newsitem.title: UK: Zinc prices near a 2-year high, coffee also gains.
newsitem.headline: Zinc prices near a 2-year high, coffee also gains.

text.p: A powerful rally in the world price of zinc accelerated on Wednesday and took the metal to its highest price in almost two years on the London Metal Exchange.
Traders said renewed fund and speculator buying helped three months delivery zinc to $1,132 per tonne for a gain of about seven percent since the beginning of the year,

Prices for zinc, a metal mainly used in the galvanising process, took off this week after news that LME-supervised warehouse stocks declined by 11,975 tonnes to 487,325 in the latest week, to the lowest since December 1992.
"LME zinc stocks have now recorded 29 consecutive month-on-month drawdowns," said Nick Moore, analyst with Flemings Global Mining Group.

Stocks have dropped by 60 percent since October 1994 when they peaked at 1.24 million tonnes. But some metals analysts add that the rally, which has been led by fund buyers, could meet resistance from selling out of China. China already produces a surplus and may expand its output.
Zinc ended in London at $1,123, up $13 from Tuesday.
Nickel and aluminium were firmer and copper was steady.

Gold extended a sharp decline that has marked the start of 1997, on speculator fears of central bank bullion sales like that announced by the Dutch this week of 300 tonnes. Gold closed in London at $354.15 an ounce, down $3.40 but up from a 3-1/4 year low bid of $351.80.

Oil prices were also easier with the bellwether Brent Blend of North Sea crude trading around $23.15 per barrel late in London's Wednesday afternoon. Fears that winter fuel demand might squeeze low world stocks of oil are abating.

Coffee futures again extended a rally, supported by news of low U.S. stocks and a dockworkers' strike in Colombia that slowed exports there. The London March robusta coffee futures contract reached an intra-day high at $1,335 per tonne which was a gain from Tuesday of $20, before it eased slightly toward the close.

African coffee producers urged Asian states Indonesia and Vietnam to back a plan to trim coffee exports and lock in higher prices which will be aired at emergency producer talks to be held in Brazil on January 23.
"Africa still has coffee as its lifeline," Guy-Alain Gauze, chairman of the InterAfrican Coffee Organisation (IACO) and Ivorian Commodities Minister, told a conference in Vietnam.
Traders said both Indonesia and Vietnam had been lukewarm to IACO's plan for a cut in Association of Coffee Producing Countries' (ACPC) exports in the first half of 1997.
